SECRETARY’S REPORT. 


The thirty-seventh year of the history of this Association has 
had the manifest approval and blessing of God. The full inter- 
pretation of this progressive work for young men has been 
hindered by the limited capacity of our present building; but all 
the departments undertaken have been crowded, and the results 
secured call for increased facilities and equipment. 

The general policy of the past year has been—first, the 
education and development of the younger ‘men and their direc- 
tion in lines of Christian work, and second, the influencing towards 
the Christian life of our associate members. The reports as 
presented will present a steady advance in every department. 


EDUCATIONAL. 


The Libraries and Reading Room have been taxed to their 
utmost capacity; showing an average daily attendance of 475. 
This represents 142,900 visits by young men during the year. 
To direct rightly the reading habits of a young man is, in the 
majority of cases, to save him from ruin. This department needs 
an endowment of at least $5,000. After carefully observing the 
results from our limited Library, we do not know of any place 
where money could be invested as wisely. The Circulating 
Library contains 2802 volumes, has had 659 readers, and an issue 
of 6603 books. 


The Evening Classes are carried on under many disadvantages ; 
still the seven weekly Classes enrolled 371 members. This 
branch appeals to all as one of the best methods to help young 
men to help themselves. The old system of apprenticeship once 
so beneficial, is now practically unknown: a young man was 
bound for four or five years, and besides teaching him the busi- 
ness in all its branches, his master had some care over the habits 
and life of the apprentice. One of the evil results of the present 
system is seen from the fact that out of 1160 convicts in one 


i 


8 


Penitentiary, only 136 had any trade or served an apprentice- 
ship. This department should be thoroughly equipped. It 
affords an opportunity for commercial and mechanical training 
which will secure for them early promotion and open the way for 
further advancement. 


PHYSICAL, 


Without a Gymnasium, and without suitable Recreation 
Grounds but little progress can be made in this department. 
A Lacrosse club “practised” three mornings weekly during the 
summer. The “Excelsior Snow Shoe Club” was composed. of 
members who made‘weekly “tramps” over the mountain to the 
room in the Athletic Club House. The Junior Snow Shoe Club 
held their tramps on Saturday afternoons. Through affiliation 


with Mr. Barnjum’s Gymnasium, a number of the members. 


entered his classes for physical culture. 


The Employment Bureau had 655 applications for employ- 
ment, and secured 185 situations. 


We have again and again protested against several of the 
Societies who send out men penniless, and not having a trade or 
any definite line of work they are helpless. We have to decline 
assistance in the great majority of these cases. In this con- 
nection there is the greatest necessity for some cheap Temperance 
Lodging and Eating House where young men working for low 
wages could be accommodated. 


Other Associations are securing athletic grounds for recreation. 
As the city extends, this becomes more difficult and almost 
impossible. It is therefore a question which should receive a 
attention of the directors. 


SOCIAL. 


The social element has increased. The Building has become 
more popular and attractive asa place of resort, apart from 
meetings or business. The Reception Committee has greatly 
aided in promoting sociability amongst the members and the 
committeemen of all departments. 


es ee ee 


9 


The New Year’s Reception drew 800 young men to the 
building. 


The Members’ Monthly Meeting has had an average attend- 
ance of 175—ladies from the various Churches rendering 
invaluable aid. 


The “ Strangers’ Tea” has been a new feature, commenced the 
first Sunday in March. Asa means of introducing strangers in 
the city to the Association, and afterwards to the Churches, it will 
be a valuable adjunct to the work. 


Mrs. E. H. Botterell very kindly gave her home for a Parlor 
Concert on Feb. 16th,secured the programme, and as a result 
netted over $100 used in Parlor furnishings. She has the thanks 
of the Association for her interest in this work. 


In this department on one evening each week there should be 
planned an informal Social Hour,—the time being spent in song 
and conversation. making it the place of introduction between 
each new member and the Reception Committee. This would 
become popular, and of practical value. Let it be tried. 


‘THE JUNIOR DEPARTMENT 


has made the most marked progress. On account of limited 
accommodation the work has been confined to the Friday evening 
and a Monday evening Training Class. The average attendance 
Friday evenings has been 100, and 40 or 50 are Christian lads. 
The Cote St. Antoine Branch has been firmly established. The 
leaders command the love and confidence of the boys, and are 
rendering them important help by unconscious influence through 
personal contact. The future leaders of the Association are 
being trained here. | 


For the next fall and winter another Branch should be estab- 
lished in the northern part of the city. The boy’s section in the 
Library should be increased, and a wisely planned course of 
Practical Talks upon commercial and mechanical subjects should 
be carried out. 


IO 


We may be in some measure’responsible for the impression 
which is abroad that the Association work is wholly on behalf of 
the stranger class of young men, and for the rescue of the fallen. 
That is certainly a work which it delights to do; but its chief 
efforts should always be directed on the line of “prevention.” 
Not only does it reach after the stranger young man, but it is a 
mission: to the GOOD BOYS in our homes, offering the best safe- 
guard to the many temptations which appeal to them, and show- 
ing the brighter and better way to a healthy, manly, Christian 
character. Let this department receive the best consideration 
from the directors. 


THE RELIGIOUS WORK 


is the chief department. In fact we hesitate to make the dis- 
tinction between the secular and the religious ; because every 
branch is carried on in order that we may win young men to the 
loyal allegiance of our Master, Jesus Christ. The testimony of 
facts prove that by means of the Employment Bureau, the 
Temperance Pledge, the Boarding House Register, the Libraries, 
the Training Classes, the Practical Talks, the Invitation and 
Reception work, young men have been led to make the surrender 
of their lives to Christ. — iiss 

A staff of one hundred and forty-seven young men have served 
on the various committees. The Young Men’s Meeting has 
obtained an average of 95, higher than any previous year ; the 
Bible Study Class for beginners on Sunday morning has had an 
average attendance of 35; the Young Men’s Evangelistic Bible 
Class has increased its average from 59 last year to 85 this year. 
Two Training Classes for Christian workers have been conducted 
from October to April. We have held in this building 603 
religious meetings, with an attendance of 21,884 young men. 

A marked advance is noted in the line of Bible Study, and the 
result is seen in a stronger and more intelligent staff of workers. 

The Associate members have claimed our first attention; 
through a corresponding member in each Church they have been 
introduced to the Church and Sunday School immediately on 


ai 


joining the Association, and through a band of workers a large 
number have received a personal call, inviting them to attend the 
Young Men’s Meetings or Bible Classes. The results of this 
work warrants its continuance in a more thorough and system- 
atic manner. . Enquirers at the various meetings have been 
promptly introduced to the Pastors of Churches they attended 
or preferred. 

The Hospital service has beén regularly carried on by faithful 
workers. 


The Militia Camp was stationed at Granby last July for 12 
days. The “Association Tent” with its equipment is now a 
recognized part of the Camp. The nightly services were 
crowded, and 87 of the men made personal inquiry as to 
spiritual life. 


The distribution of tracts amongst the seamen on Sunday 
mornings was continued during the season. Also three meetings 
were held weekly for seamen at the Institute. 


The present need is a larger staff of consecrated, intelligent 
workers, who are all-the-year-round men. We have many ; but 
the work calls for more. The Young Men’s Meeting and Bible 
Classes offer one of the best fields in the city for personal work, 
and those who are willing patiently to follow up the cases of 
young men, one by one, until they are brought out into the liberty 
of the Christian life, can here find a most happy and useful 
sphere, and lay up a rich foundation against the time to come. 


The Board should provide for a series of Evangelistic meet- 
ings for young men to be held in September or October of each 
year. Let this be a regular opening of the Fall work. 


We report with pleasure, that Mr. J. P. EDWARDS,a former 
' member, whose conversion occurred here, and his early training 
in Christian work, enters the Springfield School for training as a 
Secretary in September. Mr. W. T. HART, formerly a member 
here, enters the Chicago Association as office Secretary. In the 
past 12 years the roll has now grown to 28 young men, (besides 
those left at home,) who have through this Association gone out 


12 
into active Christian work,—either as pastors of churches, evan- 
gelists, or secretaries of Associations. May the number be 
doubled in the next 12 years, of those who will be thrust out into 
the great harvest field—for winning the young men of this land 
for Christ. 


A new departure is the sending of MR. ARTHUR BEALL, B.A., 
of Queen’s College, Kingston, as a Missionary Teacher to Japan. 
He may possibly be joined by a second man, to be sent out 
this year under the auspices of the Association. Let our con- 
tinued prayers follow these brethren in this work. 


Mr. W. H. STEVENS, for more than two years Assistant Sec- 
retary, resigned to accept the Secretaryship of the’ Peterboro’ 
Association, where he is doing a good work. His place has been 
filled by Mr. D. W. CORBETT, called into Christian life through 
this Association during the past year, and who is rapidly develop- 
ing into a most efficient worker. 


Mr. T. DUNCAN PATTON, Chairman of our Invitation Com- 
mittee has entered the office as Librarian and Assistant Secretary. 


Mr. HAROLD W. BUCHANAN, for ten years chairman of the 
Boys’ work, was called to the position on Assistant Secretary in 
the New York Association. 


The Association heartily responded to the call of the union 
committee of Pastors,and rendered every possible assistance at 
the Moody meetings. The result of the fortnight services in 
October was a great blessing to the Christian life of the city, and 
especially to the young men. 


/ 


NEW BUILDING SITE. 


We have to record two events in the history of the Association: 
Furst:—The purchase of the incorporated rights of the Montreal 
Auxiliary Bible Society, Canada Sunday School Union, and 
Religious Tract Society, for the sum of $12,000, and one-fifth of 
any amount above $60,000 for which the building may be sold. 
Second:—For three years past the Directors have been searching 
for a future building site. Every effort seemed fruitless until the 


13 


Moody Meetings in the Crystal rink, when they were providen- 
tially directed to that central position. On May 4th the deed 
was signed, and the first payment of $5000 made, so that this 
magnificent site is now the property of the Young Men’s 
Christian Association, of Montreal. With the good hand of our 
God upon us in further blessings we shall hope to enter the new 
building, dedicated to the best interests of the young men of the 
metropolis of the Dominion, not later than May Ist, 1890. 


Every room in our present building will live in our memories. 
It has been hallowed as a spot where thousands of lives have 
met Jesus, the young man of Nazareth, and by his power have 
been changed from bondage into liberty, and from darkness into 
light. Let us not forget to do honor to the friends,—the fore- 
most among whom was Mr. T. James Claxton,—whose faith 
prompted them to erect this beautiful building,and who have 
had such a good return in the results of the past 14 years. 


Doubtless some of our friends who may not be fully informed 
as to the progress of the Young Men’s Christian Association. 
work on this continent are criticizing the wisdom of this move- 
ment ; but facts prove that such is the adaptability of our work 
to the present needs of young men, that three or four such 
buildings in every city could be successfully manned to the best 
interests of the Church and the community. Let these figures 
be considered : one hundred and twenty-five Associations now 
own buildings in value amounting to $6,500,000, and the property 
is increasing at the rate of $1,000,000 each year; some cities 
having four or five branch buildings in addition to the central. 
Since January, 1887,new buildings have been dedicated as follows: 
Toronto, $90,000; Indianapolis, $80,000: Albany, $100,000 ; 
Detroit,$125,000; St. Joseph, Miss., $100,000; Worcester, Mass., 
$140,000; Atlanta, Ga., $80,000; New Britain, Conn., $50,000; 
Wichita, Kan., $50,000; Rockford, III., $30,000; Norfolk, Va., 
$30,000 ; Nashville, Tenn., $75,000; Burlington, Vt., $40,000. 
Buildings are now in course of erection, or the work about to 
begin : at Ottawa, $25,000; Morristown, N. J., $20,000; Utica, 


14 


N.Y., $80,000; Los Angelos, Cal., $75,000; Pascenda, $60,000 ; 
San Diago, $75,000; Riverside, $25,000; Omaha, Neb., $100,000; 
Kansas City, $100,000; Denver, Col., $120,000; St. Paul, Minn., 
$150,000 ; Minneapolis, Minn., $125,000 ; Providence, R. I, 
$150,000; Cleveland, $130,000. There are, in addition, over 100 
other building enterprises in course of development. These 
subscription lists show that sums varying from $1000 to $250,000 
have been given by single individuals, men who are broad in 
their sympathies, strong supporters of their Church, and who 
realize in this cause an opportunity for an investment which must 
yield a large return in the immediate future,—a return which 
must strengthen and increase every phase of Christian and 
philanthropic work. Christian men are giving these amounts 
because they see that the Associations are used by God in com- 
bating the evils which crowd around city life. In fact the 
burning question of to-day, political as well as moral, is the 
future of these great cities, and how to counteract the thousands 
of places of evil resort which absorb the time and the money of 
the young men. The facts are appalling. This goodly land is 
strewn with wrecks, both of the bodies and souls of the fairest of 
its young men, who might have been saved to their homes, the 
Church and the world, had they but formed the right associates, 
between the ages of 16 and 21. 3 


Who, then, of Montreal’s liberal hearted, practical, Christian 
men and women will come forward, and according to their 
ability, share in placing on Dominion square, a building erected 
free from debt, thoroughly furnished for the present and future 
requirements of the work. Before the close of 1889 we shall be 
disappointed if the amount required is not fully subscribed. 
In Cleveland, one citizen headed the list with $25,000, on condition 
that the balance required was subscribed within six months. The 
board will be glad to receive any of that description !

OF THE 


COMMITTEES OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS. 


FINANCE. 


The work of your Committee has been aided by the liberal and hearty response 
on the part of merchants and citizens. As the work is better understood it becomes 
more appreciated. The careful canvass of each district calls for much time in the 
busiest part of the day ; but this has been cheerfully given by the members of the 
Committee. The work demands a larger number of collectors, and additional mem- 
bers should be secured. The contributors will please accept the thanks of the Finance 
Committee. Mr. Arthur G. Olive has carefully supervised the book-keeping during — } 
the year. The Association is indebted to him for this service. Messrs. George Creak 
and J. B. Picken have made a careful audit of the accounts, for which the thanks of 


the Association is tendered. 
WARDEN KING, 


Chairnuian.

22 


ROOMS AND LIBRARY. 


The labors of the Committee have not been so arduous as in some former years, 
owing largely to the very efficient librarian, assistant secretary, and caretaker. 


A “condenser” was added to our heating boiler, which has largely increased the e 
amount of heat furnished. 


New chairs were purchased for the use of meetings, and some new furniture has 
been added to the parlor, and some games have been placed therein for the use of 4 
members and their friends. The parlor is now open at all times for a quiet .chat or 4 
game of chess or draughts, or an hour’s study or reading. i 


The reading room has had an attendance of about 475 per day, showing that this 
branch of the work is much appreciated. By a careful count we find that more than _ 
one-half of the young men who enter the rooms daily are members,—the others are q 
largely strangers in the city. | i 


Several magazines and papers have been added to our files, aud our tables now a 
present a fine assortment of reading matter. i" 


Your Committee are happy to report a steady increase in the number of volumes o 
taken from the library during the year, and in the number. of readers. During the — 
season of the Educational classes there is a large demand for books upon the various a 
subjects studied, a greater demand than we have been able to supply. It would bea * 
great boon to the students if a number of technical works could be placed on our a 
shelves. One, and a most cheering feature of the library work has been the great ‘ 
number of boys who make use of its privileges. There must be more than 150 a 
readers of this class. The question of reading matter for boys is a most important r 
one, and if, through this Association, we can successfully cater to their needs, it will a 
not only do a good work directly, but will indirectly raise up a large number of friends q 
for its future support. q

EXECUTIVE. 


The Executive Committee has held sixteen meetings during the past year. 


Our late Assistant Secretary, Mr. Stevens, left us in September last, to take the 
position of Secretary of the Peterboro’ Association, and we are glad to hear he is doing 
successful work there. Your Committee secured Mr. D. W. Corbett as his successor 
and assistant to Mr. Budge, and his six months’ service has proved him an efficient 
and acceptable worker for young men. 


The thirty-sixth anniversary was held in Erskine Church, twenty-sixth January 
Jast, and was addressed by Rev. F. H. Marling, and Hon. S. H. Blake, of Toronto. 
The large and enthusiastic gathering is an index of the increased interest which our 
work for young men is producing in the minds of the Christian public of this city. 


At one of Mr. Moody’s meetings in October last, a special collection was taken 
to send a teacher to Japan. Mr. A. W. Beall, B.A., has been secured, and he will 
sail via Vancouver, B.C., on July 3ist. 


We are glad to report that all the employees in the various branches of our work 
co-operate heartily with each other, and that there is an active spiritof holy consecra- 
tion in many of our young men, which must result in attracting other young men into 


the service and love of our Lord Jesus Christ. 
D. BENTLEY, 


Chatrman.

COMMITTEES OF THE ASSOCIATION. 


SOCIAL, RELIGIOUS MEETINGS. 
YOUNG MEN’S MEETING. 


s 
The interest and attendance has shown increase—the average being 95 for the — 
year. The subjects presented have all been well chosen and ably treated by our | 
chairmen. A feature worthy of notice is the fact that several of those who led our 
meetings acted as chairmen for the first time. This has become the great training — 


school for future work in the Association. 


The meeting on Christmas eve was one long to be remembered. Thesubject was. f 
“ Past, Present and Future.” The addresses of Messrs. Packard, Putnam and Meyers” 
were most appropriate, and must have created a strong impression. 4 


The personal work at the close of the meeting is the special need, and the names 
of those who make this enquiry are immediately forwarded to the pastors. " 

A young man who received one of our printed invitations at an hotel recently, | 
came to the meeting, and at the close stated in conversation that the meeting was a_ 
revelation to him. To seea company of young men so interested in the study of 
God’s Word, and able so readily to turn from one portion of Scripture to another, was — 
something he could scarcely understand, and in parting he expressed his intention to 
look more seriously into these things for himself. 


The point to be secured is the attendance of the Associate Members, as - this] | 
meeting is specially for them. This has been overtaken in some measure by personal , 
visitation by committee men ; but it should be doneso that every associate would — 


visited. j J 4 q 
GEORGE S. RoORKE, a 


Chairman. 5 


25 
BOYS’ DEPARTMENT. 


The efforts of this Committee to carry on a successful work among the ‘‘ juniors ” 
of our Association have been abundantly blessed and owned of God. 


The attendance during the winter months has averaged over one hundred. The 
majority of the boys attending are converted. Over thirty profess to have entered 
upon the Christian life at our Friday evening gatherings. Each member brings his 
own Bible, and it is a glad sight to see the manly little fellows turning its leaves to 
chapter and verse and taking part in the topic of the evening. 


Apart from the regular work of the ‘‘ Boy’s Branch” the features of the year has 
been the opening of a Branch in December last, at 3225 St. Catherine street, Cote St. 
Antoine, where the interest and attendance has steadily increased from 7 to45. In 
April last, this Branch held a social in Cote St. Antoine Academy, over which the 
Mayor, Mr. Thos. Patton, presided. The hall was packed with the most lively and 
interesting crowd of boys that ever assembled within its walls. ‘I'wenty-five dollars 
towards the new building fund was one of the results. The Saevengs Bank is also a 
new and important feature in our work. During the winter a very successful Sxow- 
Shoe Club was carried on among the boys, who enjoyed the sport immensely. Fifty 
dollars worth of prizes were donated and distributed at the close of the season to 
successful competitors. 


A missionary spirit prevails among our lads. Every month the General Hospital 
is visited by them, and boys loaded with magazines and picture books for the little ones 
and other good things, make a tour of the wards, also helping in the Sunday morning 
service for nurses and patients. Last year $5 was voted to the Indian boys’ school at 
Sault Ste. Marie, and this year the Montreal Boys’ Home receives a contribution and 
a sum of money voted towerds the new building. 


The Scripture Union has also increased in membership, over 1100 having joined 
during the year. This part of the work is under the management of Mr. C. H. 
Anderson. During the past year we have lost two of our boys, called away by the 
Master to the great meeting above ; both died trusting in Jesus. Mr. Harold W. 
Buchanan, our late chairman, removed to New York to work among the boys there. 
We take this opportunity to thank our friends for the beautiful large crayon drawing 
of Mr. Buchanan which hangs in the boys’ room. 


Five socials and a picnic were given during the year in connection with our 
meetings, the boys themselves largely contributing. | Thanks are due to the ladies 
for their kind help on these occasions, and to Mr. D. W. Ross for the use of his home 
for the Branch meetings. 


During the winter a special training class under the leadership of Mr. George C. 
Wells has been held for the Christian lads, meeting on Monday evenings in the cil ed 
room to study God’s Word. ‘This has been the secret of our success. 


JOSEPH GAWNE, 
Chairman.

MEMBERSHIP. 


This Committee have much pleasure in reporting that 430 young men have joined 4 
the Association during the past year, which shows an increase of 170 over the year end. q 
ing May, 1887. When we consider that these young men have joined the Association — i 
of their own accord, without canvassing, it gives an idea of the grow ing popularity of # 
the work. Had we had sufficient room to receive all the applicants for the winter a 
classes, this number would have been largely increased ; as it was, a large number hat 
to be turned away. Of the 430 members added, 118 were enrolled as active, and 312 
as associate.

cities, deaths, withdrawals, etc.

SOCIAL WORK. 


Upon this Committee devolves the development in a great measure of the social _ 
element amongst old and new members. For this purpose a musical and literary pro- 
gramme is arranged for, and rendered each month in the parlor. 


The Committee have great pleasure in acknowledging the help of the ladies of 
the following Churches, who kindly provided and served refreshments after the pro-. a 
gramme :—American Presbyterian, Dominion Square Methodist, Erskine Presby- — 
terian, Stanley Street Presbyterian, Mountain Street Methodist, Knox Presbyterian, 
and Emmanuel Congregational. Perhaps the most important feature of this regular 
monthly meeting is the address by the ministers of the different churches. 
The parlors were tastefully decorated on New Year’s day, and refreshments 
served to callers. In the evening a most enjoyable entertainment was given, the place 
being thronged with friends of the young men and sympathizers in their work. 
G. F. GoppArp, 4 
Chairman, — 


27 
EMPLOYMENT WORK. 


There have been 655 applications for employment during the past year, or an 
average of 244 over the year ending May, 1887. Of these, 183 secured employment 
directly through the efforts of the Bureau, besides many others were counselled and 
advised. We have been as careful as possible in looking out for good men to recom- 
mend for vacancies. To enable us to do this, we have an enquiry blank which we 
send to applicants’ previous employers, and the answer generally enables us to act 
intelligently. 

We consider that this is one of the most useful methods in the Association work 
for personally reaching young men. We first of all endeavor to secure them employ- 
ment and win their confidence. When they see you are interested in their worldly 
affairs they will generally attend the meetings when asked. Quite a number have been 
won for the Master through this medium, some of whom are engaged in active work 
of the Association. One of the pleasing features in the department is the general 
satisfaction these men have given their employers. 


We have always a number of efficient men on hand, and we shall be pleased to 
have the continued co-operation of the business men of this city on their behalf. 


The following statement shows the work accomplished during the past year :

EVANGELISTIC BIBLE CLASS. 


The Committee of the Evangelistic Bible Class which is held every Sunday after- g 
noon at 3 o’clock, have much pleasure in reporting that the past year has been one of _ | 
marked advancement. At no time has this class shown its usefulness more than during | 
the past six or eight months. if 

The average attendance has increased from 59 to 85. During the winter months. _ 4 
it has been especially good, often reaching above'100. This we consider due to the q 
fact that all are doing personal work in bringing others. The Class is composed yo 
mostly of young men from 18 to 35 years of age. F ; 

The lessons which have been so attractive were from the Old Testament. One 
lesson in January, and one in April on Social Purity have been followed by vera 
gratifying results. 

Although this class is mainly Evangelistic, the lessons are so applied that it is a 
grand training class for teachers and others who intend taking up Christian work. 
Some have left us during the past year to become Sunday-School teachers. = 

A pleasant feature in connection with the past year’s work was a social re-union — 
heldin April. About 200 were present. 

True spiritual work is being done in this Class. Every Sunday one or more are 
brought to a kowledge of sin, and led to shelter their lives more fully under the 
shadow of the Rock Christ Jesus. 4 

We are greatly indebted to Mr. John Lomax, who has during the entire year pres 4 
sided at the organ, and rendered cheerful assistance in the service of song. 4 

The following extracts from letters received testify to benefits derived : 4 

‘‘I have been greatly benefited and blessed by attending the Class this winter. ; 
It has given me a deeper interest in Bible study than I had before....This Class has. | 
been very helpful to me in my Christian life, and I desire to thank the Lord for it.” a 

‘“‘It has given me a desire for a greater knowledge of God’s Word, which I hope 
this year to strengthen by making time to read and study more of the Bible. It has 
cheered me throngh the week and been a great help to me in business. ..I have been 
influenced by the leader to lay by a portion of my earnings each week, in which I find — 
great joy in doing... It was through the means of this Class that my conversion occur~ q 
red some few years ago.” a 


og 
( 


‘“T have often gone to the Class very much discouraged, but have left it in a vera 
different spirit, caused by the encouraging remarks. One thing I am thankful for 1s 


that I am learning more of Christ.” 
T. DUNCAN PATTON, 


Chairman. — 


SUNDAY MORNING BIBLE CLASS. 


Early last fall our leader, Mr. Stevens, was called to the Secretaryship of — 
Peterboro’ Association. The committee in looking for a successor decided upon q 
Mr. Meyers,—this busiest of men in the Master’s vineyard,—who did not hesitate to 
accept the position. He has now been with us for over seven months and we have © 


ee 2 


29 


‘been wonderfully blessed, as he has opened to us the Epistle to the Hebrews. Owing 
to press Of work, both temporal and spiritual, Mr. Meyers has had to resign. Weare 
indeed sorry to lose him as our leader ; but he will still continue to be with us as his 
health and work permits. Mr. Corbett, assistant secretary, having accepted the 
position, we ask for him the hearty co-operation of all who can attend the class. 
Westill continue our praise and service for 20 minutes before the lesson, which is 
a great help to all, especially to those who have just commenced the Christian life. 
_ We cannot say what the results of this class are ; but we know that those who 
are constantly confessing Christ and are diligent students of God’s Word must bring 
forth fruit. It may be growthin grace, love for souls, or more consecration to Christ’s 


service. 
a 


J. WILSON, 
Chairman. 


INVITATION. 


This work shows its value to the Association in the following points :— 

First—It is the means through the Invitations distributed on the street corners 
and hotels of bringing in numbers of young men to our meetings, and many by God’s 
grace have here found Salvation. We may here mention one case which has come 
prominent before us during the past year. A young man passing along the street on 
Saturday evening received an invitation to our young men’s meeting with the follow- 
ing question on it: ‘‘ Where will you spend eternity?” As he walked along some 
distance he could find no rest, as he could not answer the question, and finally resolved 
to come to the meeting, during which he was convicted of sin and remained at the 
close, enquiring the way of life. The next Sunday morning at the Bible Class he gave 
the above testimony, and he is now engaged in Christian work in the east end of 
ithe city. 

The work of the committee is divided into different sections. /%st.—The dis- 
tribution of invitations for the young men’s meeting on Saturday evening ; second—the 
distribution of invitations for the young men’s bible Class Sunday afternoon. The 
number of Invitations distributed for the foregoing sections was about 50,000. The 
third section of our work is to keep the ‘‘ take-one-boxes ” that have been placed in 
the principal hotels and railroad waiting rooms full of tracts, the ‘‘ Association Record,” 
Invitation cards of our meetings, etc. We hope that through this means these Gospel 
messages may be a blessing to many souls. We are just organizing a fourth branch 
of this work, which is to keep a Register of all the Protestant young men in the prin- 
cipal commercial and manufacturing houses of the city, and we hope to bring the 
advantages of the Association before them either by mail or a personal call. 

The Committee considered during the year the necessity of having a framed card, 
with all the meetings of the Association, placed in the hotels and principal steamboats, 
and hope soon to see this accomplished. 

S. MUIRHEAD, 
Chairman. 


30 
RECEPTION. 


Since September, through the influence of this Committee 47 young men have 


been asked to become members. Twenty-eight have joined the Association, 138 have © , 


been invited to attend the regular meetings, 25 have been spoken to in reference to 
their soul’s welfare, and 15 have been welcomed from other Associations. During 
the Moody meetings your committee had charge of the ushering, and were on hand 
every evening, and often three times a day, and this without neglecting the Association 
work, required no small amount of self-denial. A number of games have been added 
to the parlor attractions which have been much appreciated. 

The duties of members of the committee are as follows .— 
To be at the rooms from 7.30 to Io p.m. daily, to receive the young men coming 
in (especially if they are strangers) giving them a word of welcome, and a hearty 
shake of the hand, showing them through the building, introducing them to the sec- 
retaries and members, and in doing all they can to make them feel at home, not 
neglecting (if opportunity should occur) to speak a word for the Master. 


a 


ALEX. ARTHUR, 
Chairman. 


STRANGERS’ TEA. 


A new feature of our Association work is the Strangers’ Tea which was started 
in the beginning of March, and takes place every Sunday afternoon. The object of 
the meeting is to welcome the young men who come as strangers to the city, to pro- 
vide them with Christian fellowship, and to introduce them to some church in the city. 

The average attendance for | | 


Committee. Strangers. Total. ¢ 
March 3. ins ge Cee 5 ape tio ae 24 
Aprib, pasa ws iP WR ipa robete Fay ek dae’ 26 
Magy sisi gs Me Dailies Or aia. dus 36 


The strangers meet shortly before five, and a few hymnsare sung, after which tea is 
served, the members of the committee attending to the wants of the guests. While sit- 


ting at the table, each one in turn introduces himself by telling his name, where he comes 
from, what church he belongs to, and how long he has been in the city. After tea an 


adjournment is made to the parlor, where more hymns are sung, and one of the Direct- 
ors, after reading a portion of Scripture, gives a short, earnest, Christian talk, with 
some warm words of welcome and encouragement for the strangers. The meeting is 
then thrown open for a short time, and any one is at liberty to say a few words, give 
out a hymn, etc. The members of the committee who represent all the various 
denominations afterwards bring the visitors to their respective churches, and see that 
they are introduced to the pastor. 

The interest in the meeting has been very marked, and even during the short — 
time it has been held, we have been greatly encouraged by the testimony of many, as 
to the help and encouragement received at the time of loneliness, when it is most he 
needed and thoroughly appreciated. : |

J. S. HETHERINGTON, P

COMMERCIAL TRAVELLERS. 


During the past few months an effort has been made to create amongst the com- 
mercial travellers in this city an interest in this Association, and its work throughout 
the Dominion. The Committee regret that the work is not far enough advanced to 
be enabled to give a very satisfactory report, but we are glad to say already we have 
seen fruits of the work, and hope during the coming year that this department will be 


got into successful working order. 
Tuos. R. FLINT, 


Chazrnuian. 


TRACT DISTRIBUTION AMONG SAILORS. 


This work commenced the second Sunday in May, meeting in the Sailors’ 
Institute at 7.45 a.m. each Sunday morning, and continued to the end of November. 
The field of labor extends from Windmill Point to Hochelaga, under a band of 
from 14 to 17 workers, each worker having a section under his charge ; the attendance 
throughout the summer being very good. The results from this service are difficult to 
estimate, other than the opportunity it gives for sowing the seed, and with personal 
contact with so large a class of men, in the ministry of the Gospel. 


WILLIAM Law, 
Chatrman. 


“EXCELSIOR” SNOW SHOE CLUB. 


_ It must be admitted that while a Christian ought always to be busy in the cause 
of his Divine Master, yet young men with healthy bodies and active minds need activity 
and recreation. But a wise selection of a field of activity and healthy amusement, 
instead of making him less efficient and sincere in his Christian duty, should make 
him all the better fitted for it, and it is therefore of the greatest importance that such 
means of physical culture and amusement should be chosen as will help to improve 
mind and body. 

Those of our members who tramped on Snow-shoes over the mountain will 
testify that they were invigorated by the exercise. We met every Friday evening 
during the winter, at the corner of Sherbrooke and Peel streets, and tramped to the 
Athletic Club House, where we spent an hour, entertaining each other with song and 
recitation, or with games of the nature of Foot-ball. Such exercise and enjoyment 
with congenial companions is natural, desirable and proper for young men with healthy 
constitutions, and we feel that the Y. M. C. A. are doing a wise thing when they 
encourage the members in gymnastics and out-door manly sports. Looking hopefully 
to the prospects of having a fully equipped gymnasium, we feel assured that the pos- 
session of suitable athletic grounds also would be of very great value to the young 


men, and to the best interests of the Association. 
Gro. W. JONES, 


Chatrman.

AN ACT 


to amend and consolidate the Acts relating to the Young Men’s Christian Association 
of the City of Montreal. 


Assented to June, 1888. 


WHEREAS the Young Men’s Christian Association of M ontreal, incorporated by 
the act 34 Vict., chap. 59, and amended by the acts 36 Vict., chap. 63, and 48 Vict., 
chap. 49, has by its petition represented that it has purchased from the Montreal 
Auxiliary Bible Society, Canada Sunday School Union, and Religious Tract Society, 
all the rights and privileges sechred to them by the said acts in its present building and 
property, and that the said institution fulfils the objects of its foundation and has greatly 
extended its operations ; so that it has become necessary to remove from the premises 
now occupied by it to more central and larger premises, and to establish branches in 
different parts of the city of Montreal and suburbs, and in order to better define its 
powers and remove all doubts as to the same, it is expedient to amend and consolidate 
the act incorporating it, and it is expedient to grant the prayer of the said petition ; 
Therefore, Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Legislature at 
Quebec, enacts as follows : 


1. The Young Men’s Christian Association of Montreal has been and shall con- 
tinue to be a body corporate and politic under said name. 


2. The object of the said corporation has been, is, and shall be the improvement 
of the spiritual, mental, social and physical condition of young men, by the maintenance 
of libraries, reading rooms, lectures, classes, social and religious services, and such other 
means as may promote this object. 


3. The affairs, work, and property of the corporation shall be administered and 
managed by a board of twenty-one directors, who shall be elected and hold office for 
three years, or until their successors are elected, one third of whom shall retire annually, 
but shall be eligible for re-election. 

The board shall be chosen from the active members of the corporation, and not 
more than one-third shall belong to any one denomination. 

The present members of the board of directors shall continue in office until their 
successors are elected. 


4. All property now owned by, or which may be acquired by purchase, gift, devise or 
bequest or any other title shall be held in the corporate name of the said corporation ; 
but the immoveable property shall not be sold, hypothecated, or otherwise alienated or 
charged, unless it be consented to by a majority of the active membership present at a 
meeting specially called for that purpose, fourteen days’ notice thereof having been 
given, by two insertions in each of one morning and one evening daily paper published 
in the city of Montreal, and also with the consent of three-fourths of the directors, such 
consent to be recorded in the minute book of the Association. 


5. The said corporation may acquire, hold and use for its work and objects any 
property by any title, and may sell, alienate, hypothecate, pledge, exchange or lease it 
or any part thereof, but it shall not own real estate except that in actual use by the 
corporation, of an annual value of more than ten thousand dollars for more than five 
years at any one time. 


6. The deed of sale and agreement entered into by the said corporation, and the 
Montreal Auxiliary Bible Society, Canada Sunday School Union, and Religious Tract 
Society, and executed before Charles Cushing, N.P., on the 29th day of May, eighteen 
hundred and eighty-eight, is hereby ratified and confirmed, and declared good and 
valid ; and the said corporation is hereby declared to be the sole owner and proprietor 
of the property known as lot official number 1063 of the official plan and book of 
reference of St. Antoine Ward in the city of Montreal and the building thereon 
erected, with full power to deal therewith, subject only to the hypothec in favor of 
the said Montreal Auxiliary Bible Society as therein set forth. 


34 


4 


7. The said corporation may make and adopt such constitution, by-laws and rules 
as it may deem expedient for the conduct of its affairs and the guidance of its officers 
as are not contrary to this act or charter, or tolaw. 

Section 1., Article 1. of by-laws as now existing shall not be altered or repealed, 
in so far as it provides that only members in good standing of some Protestant evangel- 
ical church in the city of Montreal have the right to vote and hold office in the 
Association. 

The present constitution and by-laws of said corporation, except such portions as 
are inconsistent with this act, shall remain in force until changed or repealed thereunder. 

8. All the provisions the acts 34 Vict., chap. 59; 36 Vict. chap. 63 and 48 Vict., 
chap. 49, which are inconsistent with, or contrary to this act are hereby repealed and 
all portions of the constitution and by-laws of the said corporation as have been passed 
in virtue of such repealed provisions are hereby repealed. 


g. This act shall come into force on the day of its sanction. 


CONSTITUTION 


OF THE 


Young Men’s Christian Association of Montreal. 


ARTICLE I1.—NAME. 


The name of this Society shall be “ The Young Men’s Christian Association ” 
of Montreal. 
ARTICLE II.—BASsIs. 


SECTION I.—This Association seeks to unite those young men, who, regard-_ 
ing Jesus Christ as their God and Saviour according to the Holy Scriptures, 
desire to be His disciples in their doctrine and their life, and to associate their 
efforts for the extension of His kingdom amongst young men. 

SecTION II.—This Association adopts as the basis of all its proceedings 
those fundamental principles of Evangelical Christianity on which all orthodox 
Protestant Churches are agreed, and will never admit any intermeddling with 
those matters of faith and polity on which such Churches differ. 


ARTICLE JII—OBJECT. 


The object of this Association shall be the improvement of the spiritual, 
mental, social and physical condition of young men, by ways and means here- 
after designated. 

ARTICLE IV.—MEMBERS. 


Srcrion I.—The members of this Association must be young men, at least 
fourteen years of age, and shall be classed as follows : Active, Associate, Sustain- 
ing, Life and Honorary Members. 


ARTICLE V.—REAL ESTATE. 


The real estate or immovable property of the Association, as well as all funds 
of the Association, from whatsoever source derived, shall be held in_ its 
corporate name, and be managed and administered by the Board of Directors. 


; ARTICLE VI.—OFFICERS. 


Section I.—The Officers of this Association shall consist of a Board of 
Twenty-one Directors, not more than one-third of whom shall be members of any ; 
one denomination, and they shall elect a President, a Vice-President, a Treasurer 
and a Recording Secretary from among themselves, as hereafter provided. Ti 

SecTion Il.—The general objects of the Association shall be carried out — 
under the management of the Board of Directors. 


a5. 


SECTION III.—The Board of Directors shall have power to make and adopt 
Rules and By-Laws for their government, not inconsistent with the Act of Incor- 
poration or this Constitution. 


ARTICLE VII.—COMMITTEES. 


There shall be Committees of the Association appointed to carry forward its 
work, and Committees of the Board appointed to supervise the business affairs 
of the association. Special Committees may be appointed when ordered by the 
Association or the Board. The Board of Directors shall define the duties of these 
Committees, and the President shall nominate them, subject to appointment by the 
Board. The President shall be ex officio a member of all Committees. 


ARTICLE VIII.—AMENDMENTS. 


This Constitution can only be altered or amended by a vote of two-thirds (24) 
of the Active Members present at any stated meeting of the Association, provided 
such amendments shall have been previously approved of by the Board of Direc- 
tors, and have been proposed in writing at a regular meeting of the Association 
three (3) months previous to action thereupon. 


In arrange ung a separate Department for Boys Work, tt was found necessary to make some changes tn the 
By-Laws. Asa Committee of the Board of Directors, we submit the following amended By-Laws for the considera- 
tron and final action of the Association at thetr meeting on Tuesday Even zg, Nov. 20th, 1888. 


SETH P. LEET, 
DAVID BENTLEY, Commetttee. 
CHARLES CUSHING, 


BY-LAWS 


OF THE 


Young Men’s Christian Association of Montreal. 


ARTICLE I.—MEMBERSHIP. 


SECTION I.—Any young man, fourteen (14) years of age and over, who is a 
member, in good standing, of an Evangelical Church in this city, may become an 
Active member, on payment of two (2) dollars per annum, in advance. Active 
members alone shall have the right to vote and hold office. Active menbers may be 
elected at any regular monthly business meeting of the Association, provided a written 
application has been made to the Membership Committee, which has been approved 
of and recommended by them. Five negative votes shall defeat any applicant. 

SECTION II.—Any young man fourteen (14) years of age and over, of good 
moral character, may become an Associate Member on payment of two. (2) dollars per 
annum, in advance. Either the General Secretary, or in his absence the Assistant 
Secretary, may admit persons to Associate or Sustaining Membership, upon presenta- 
tion of satisfactory evidence to such officers that the applicant is a person of good 
moral character. 

SECTION III.—Any young man of good moral character may become a 
Sustaining Member by the payment in advance of five (5) dollars per annum. 
An Associate or Sustaining Member who shall unite with an Evangelical Church, 
becomes thereby an Active Member, due notice having been given to the 
Secretary. 

SECTION IV.—Life Members may be constituted by the payment of one 
hundred (100) dollars at any one time, subject to the qualifications and restrictions 
named in Article I, Section . 

SECTION V.—Honorary Members may be proposed at any regular meeting 
subject to the same qualifications and restrictions as Active and Life Members. 

SECTION VI.—Membership years shall commence on the first day of the 
month succeeding the election or admission of the member. The fiscal year of 
the Association shall commence May Ist. 


36 


SECTION VII.—Any member in arrears three (3) months for annual dues may 
be debarred all the privileges of membership, at the discretion of the Board. 

SECTION VIII.—The members of this Association shall seek out young men, 
resident or strangers, in Montreal or its vicinity, and endeavor to bring them 
under moral and religious influences, introduce them to the members and _privi- 
leges of the Association ; secure their attendance at some place of worship on the 
Sabbath, and by personal effort try to win them for Christ. They shall labor to 
induce all suitable young mento join the Association and seek to increase its 
a tae and usefulness. 


ARTICLE JI.—ELECTION OF DIRECTORS. 


SEcTION. I.—The Annual Meeting shall be held in the month of May,—one 
month’s notice shall be given of the date thereof. At this meeting there shall be chosen - 
by ballot from the members of the Association, seven, (7) Directors who shall hold 
office for three (3) years. The Board of Directors, through the Committee of Vacancies, 
shall submit a nomination of seven (7) Directors to replace those retiring, at least one 
month before the date of election, and other nominations from the Association may be © 
received at the annual meeting. Vacancies occurring during the year may be filled by 
the Board from among eligible members of the Association. 

SECTION II.—The Board of Directors at their first meeting succeeding the 
Annual Election shall elect by ballot one of their number to be President, one to be 
Vice-President, one to be Recording Secretary, and one to be Treasurer of the Board 
of the Association ; said Officers shall hold office for one (1) year, or until their success- 
ors areappointed. There shall also be appointed a General Secretary, and such other 
employés as may be needed. 

SECTION III.—The Board of Directors shall have power to elect nine (9) 
Advisory Directors who shall be members in good standing of Protestant Evangelical 
Churches, not more than one-third (4) from anyone denomination. They shall be 
notified of all meetings of the Board of Directors, and shall have the right to attend 
and participate in the discussion of all matters brought before the Board, but shall not 
be entitled to vote. Such Directors, when elected, shall be divided into three classes, 
which shall hold office respectively, one (1), two (2), and three (3) years. | Upon the 
expiration of such terms respectively, the successors of those whose terms of office 
expire shall be elected by the Board of Directors for a term of three (3) years. 


ARTICLE III.—MEETINGS OF THE BOARD. 


SECTION I.—The stated meetings of the Board shall be held on the second 
Monday evening of each month. Seven (7) shall constitute a quorum. 

SECTION II.—The following shall be the order of business :—1.—Devotional 
Exercises ; 2—Reading minutes ; 3—Unfinished Business ; 4—Treasurer’s report 3 ~ 
5—Reports of Standing Committees ; 6—Report of General Secretary ; 7—Reports . 
of Special Committees ; 8—New business. 

SECTION. III.—Special meetings of the Board may be called by the President, 
or he shall call the same at the request of three (3) Directors. The object of the 
special meeting shall be stated in the notices, and no other business shall be transacted 
except that for which the call is issued. 

SECTION IV.—If any member of the Board shall absent himself from three con- 
secutive monthly meetings of the Board, his place shall be deemed vacant, unless his 
absence shall be excused by the Board, and the vacancy may be filled. after notice is 
given to such absentee. It shall be the duty of the Recording Secretary to call the 
attention of the Board to all cases requiring action under this rule. 

SECTION V.—In order to preserve the representative character of the Board any 
member changing his denominational connection shall be deemed to have resigned, and 
the vacancy so created shall be filled as hereinbefore provided. 


- ARTICLE 1V.—DUTIES AND POWERS OF OFFICERS. 


SECTION I.—The President shall preside at all meetings of the Board. He shall 
nominate all Standing Committees, subject to appointment by the Board, to consist of 
not less than three (3) members each, and announce the same to the Board at the next 


37 


regular meeting after his election. He shall, under direction of the Board, sign all 
leases and other contracts of the Association. He shall be an ex oficto member of 
all Standing Committees of the Board and of the Association. 

SECTION II.—The Vice-President shall, in the absence of the President, have 
all the powers and perform all the duties of President. In the absence of the 
President and Vice-President, a Chairman shall be appointed from among the Board. 

SECTION III.—The Recording Secretary shall keep the minutes of all meetings 
of the Board of Directors, and shall perform such other duties as may be assigned to 
him by the Board. He shall receive and file the written reports of the various Com- 
mittees made to the Board. COs 

SECTION IV,—The Treasurer shall have charge of all funds of the Association. 
He shall present to the Board at each regular meeting a Monthly Report, and at the 
Annual Meeting in May in each year, an Annual Report of his accounts and of the 
funds of the Association. He shall pay all the demands against the Association, upon 
vouchers properly certified by the Finance Committee. He shall be’a member of the 
Finance Committee. ; 

SECTION V.—The General Secretary shall be appointed by the Board of Direc- 
tors, and shall have charge and control of the general work of the Association ; shall 
conduct all the correspondence thereof, and revise all printed matter issued thereby. 
He shall attend the meetings of the Board and the Committees of the Board, but shall 
not have the right to vote, be ex officto a member of the Committees of the Association, 
and shall attend their meetings. All other employés shall be under his supervision. 

SECTION VI.—The Board of Directors shali have the general supervision and 
control of the work and policy or the Association in all its details. All Secretaries 
and employés of any kind are to be employed and controlled solely by the Board 
of Directors. a 

SECTION VII.—If any Societies, or Organizations of any kind, are formed within 
the Association, or under its auspices, the Board of Directors shall be ex officto mem- 
bers thereof, and shall control the same as in their judgment may be necessary. 


ARTICLE VI.—STANDING COMMITTEES. 


SECTION I.—The Standing Committees of the Board shall be designated as 
follows :—1. The Executive Committee. 2. The Finance Committee. 3. The Rooms 
and Library Committee. 4. The Lecture and Classes Committee. 5. The Committee 
on vacancies. 6. The Visiting Committee for the rooms. 7. The Committee on 
Branches. 8. The Boys’ Department. 

SECTION II.—The several Committees shall keep minutes of their proceedings, 
and shall read the same as their reports to the Board at each regular meeting. No 
Committee. shall contract any indebtedness without previous appropriation of the 
Board therefor. 

SECTION III.—The Executive Committee shall have all the power of the Board 
of Directors, except that they shall not use any money of the Association, unless 
previously appropriated to them by the Board ; nor shall they have the power to 
reconsider or reserve any action of the Board had at any previous meeting. They 
shall meet at least fortnightly. They shall consider and mature plans for the general 
work of the Association, and confer and advise with the various Committees of the 
Association. They shall have the direction of the paid agents of the Association. _ 

SECTION IV.—The Finance Committee shall have charge of the financial affairs 
of the Association. At the June meeting of the Board of Directors, they shall submit 
a budget in writing, giving the estimates for the ensuing year. All bills, before pay- 
ment by the Treasurer, shall be certified by the proper officers, and approved of by 
the Committee. They shall meet at least once a month for the examination of accounts 
and other business. They shall submit a Monthly Statement to the board of 
directors. 

SECTION V.—The Rooms and Library Committee shall have charge of all rooms 
and departments of the Association, and shall establish such rules and regulations for 
the policy thereof as shall in their discretion seem best. They shall provide for the 
increase, preservation, and arrangement of the Library and reading matter in the 


38 


rooms, and for the purchase of, repairs to, and restoration of the furniture. No pub. is 
lication shall be admitted to the Library and Reading-room, unless approved of Pete 
by them. ae 

SECTION VI.—The Lecture and Classes Committee shall, subject to the approval 


of the Board, provide for the delivery of lectures. They shall have charge of the 
educational classes of the Association, shall employ teachers, and make rules and 
regulations for the same. ‘They shall visit the classes from time to time, and keep 
themselves fully informed. 
SECTION VII.—Committee on Vacancies.—Vacancies occurring in the Board of 
#Directors during the year, by resignation or otherwise, shall be filled as follows :— 
Nominations shall be made at the regular meeting of the Board, and shall be referred 
to the Committee on Vacancies, to report at the next regular meeting of the Board, 
On such a report, an election by ballot shall take place to fill the unexpired term, 
The Committee shall not recommend for election any person until they have ascertained, 
by personal enquiry of the nominee, that he is ready and willing to perform the duties 
of a Director. The Committee on Vacancies, at the meeting next preceding the 
Annual Election of the Association, shall report the names of persons to fill the places 
of those Directors whose terms of office expired by law. The names thus reported 
when approved by the Board, shall be submitted to the Association for ballot at the 
ensuing regular election. is 
SeCTION VILI.—The Visiting Committee for the Rooms shall consist of all the 
members of the Board of Directors, exclusive of the President. Two members shall 
be named for each month of the year, July and August excepted. The Secretary shall po 
furnish each Director with a list of appointments for the year, and any Director may 
furnish a substitute from among his fellow- Directors by exchange or otherwise. The 2 
Visiting Committee for the Rooms each month shall, as the official representatives of ei 
the Board, be present at the regular monthly meeting of the Association, and the 
religious meetings held at the rooms. They shall acquaint themselves with the 
religious conditions of the Association, and the working of each of the Committees, 
and shall report the same to the Board in writing. 


ARTICLE VII.—BRANCHES. 


The Board of Directors shall at such time and place as they may think advisable, 
establish and maintain branches, and shall discontinue the same at any time they may 
think best. These branches shall be under the entire control of the Board of Directors, 
under such regulations as the Board may from time to time adopt. The branches 
shall not contract any indebtedness except by authority of the Board of Directors. 


ARTICLE VIII.—RULES FOR THE ROOMS. 


SecTION. I.—The Rooms of the Association shall be opened every week-day 
from 8.30 a.m. to 10 o’clock p.m., and on the Sabbath during hours of religious service 
held in the Building. . ae 

ARTICLE [X.—MEETINGS. Bh, 

Section I.—There shall be a meeting of the Association on the third Tuesday i 
evening of each month, except in the months of July and August, when they may be ~ 
omitted if the Board of Directors so direct, for the election of members, other than 
Associate, for the promotion of social and Christian fellowship, for the presentation — 
of reports by the Association Committee, and such other exercises or business as may — 
be provided by the Board of Directors. Order of exercises :—I. Devotional. 2.3m 
Reading minutes of previous meeting. 3. Proposition and election of members. — 
4. Reports of committees. 5. Such other exercises as may be provided for. 6. — 
Adjournment. i 

SecTION II.—A Public Anniversary Meeting of the Association shall be held 
annually, the date thereof to be fixed by the Board. a 

SrecTion III.—At all the meetings of the Association, fifteen active members" 
shall constitute a quorum. ae 

Section IV.—Special meetings of the Association shall be called by»the Presi- 
dent at the written request of ten active members, or by order of the Board of Directors, 
notice being given in at least one daily paper. a 


4 


is 


39 


SECTION V.—AII meetings of the Association shall be opened by reading the 
Scripture and Prayer. No essays, or motion, of a sectarian or political character, 
shall be entertained by the Association, nor shall any denominational or political 
reference be made in any meeting of the Association or Board. 


ARTICLE X.—Boys’ DEPARTMENT. 


SECTION I.—The management of the Boys’ Department shall be vested in a 
Committee to be nominated by the President, and appointed by the Board of Directors. 
The President also shall name the Chairman. 

SECTION II.—MEMBERSHIP.—Any boy between the age of twelve (12) and 
eighteen (18) may become an Associate member of the Boys’ Department upon 
furnishing satisfactory references as to character, amd paying to the Treasurer of the 
Association the sum of one dollar per annum in advance. If the applicant is a mem- 
ber in good standing of a Protestant Evangelical Church, his name may be submitted 
to the Committee of Membership of the Association for election to Active Member- 
ship in the department. Only Active Members shall be eligible to appointment on 
the Managing Committee. 

SECTION III.—At the first meeting of this Committee they shall elect a Sec- 
retary and appoint the following sub-Committees : the Religious Meetings Commit- 
tee ; the Invitation Committee ; the Reception and Entertainment Committee ; the 
Branch Meetings Committee; the Literary Committee ; the Outing Committee, 
and with the consent of the Board of Directors such other sub-Committees as may be 
deemed necessary. 

SECTION IV.—This Committee shall see that no expenses are incurred by this 
department in excess of any appropriation which shall be made by the Board of Direc- 
tors, and shall see that no funds are solicited for the department without the approval 
of the Board. 

SECTION V.—The Committee shall have power to make and enforce rules for 
the conduct of members and visitors ‘to their Rooms, and may suspend any member 
of the department, who, in their judgment is a detriment to the department. 

SECTION. VI—This Committee shall present a written Report at each monthly 
meeting of the Board of Directors, and shall present an Annual Report immediately 
after May Ist. 

SECTION VII.—The President and the General Secretary of the Association 
shall be members ex officio of all Committees of the Department. 

MEMBERSHIP IN THE Boys’ DEPARTMENT entitles to the use of Boys’ Room, 
when opened, the Circulating Library and Literature, attendance at the Boys’ Entertain- 
ment and Lectures, participation in the Snow-Shoe Club, outings, and other sports. 


ARTICLE XI,—STANDING COMMITTEES. 


SECTION I.—The Standing Committees of the Association shall consist of not 
less than three‘members each, the chairman and members of which shall be nominated 
by the President of the Association on consultation with the General Secretary. The 
Committees shall be announced at the regular meeting of the Association following the 
annual election. 

1.—Keligious Meetings Committee ; 2.—Missions Committee ; 3.—Membership 
Committee; 4.—Employment Committee; 5.—Reception Committee; 6.—TInvitation 
Committee ;. 7.—Boarding House Committee ; 8.—Literary and Social Work Com- 
mittee; 9.—Committee on Visiting Sick Young Men; 10.—Strangers’ Tea Committee. 

SECTION II.—The Religious Meetings Committee shall have charge of all the 
regular religious meetings carried on in the Building, and shall aid the General Sec- 
retary in the religious work. This Committee may be divided into sub-committees in 
carrying out the object of its appointment. | 

SECTION III.—The Mission Committee shall have charge of all the religious 
meetings held outside the Building, except the work amongst the railway men. The 
meetings shall be held for the purpose of proclaiming the Gospel of Jesus Christ to 
lost men, and for urging its acceptance upon its hearers. : 

SECTION IV.—The Membership Committee shall devise ways and means to 
increase the membership of the Association, and shall receive all applications for active 


40 


and life membership; and after examination as to the character of each applicant shall 
report to the Association the names of those who are eligible for election. They shall 
have charge of the membership list, and shall use every effort to introduce new mem- 
bers to churches of their choice. 

SECTION V.—The Employment. Committee shall aid young men in obtaining 
employment. They shall secure information concerning applicants from former em- 
ployers and keep the same on file. They shall give full information to employers in 
’ relation to young men whom they may introduce. 

SecTION VI.—The Reception Committee shall arrange for at least one member 
on duty each evening of the week, who shall aid in making the rooms pleasant and 
attractive to members and strangers. At the close of each evening family prayers 
shall be conducted under the direction of the Committee. This Committee shall 
arrange for the ushers at the various public meetings and receptions. 

SECTION VII.—The Invitation Committee shall devise and execute plans for 
bringing young men under the influence of the Association, and securing their pres- 
ence at the religious meetings by personal solicitation, and distributing notices in the 
hotels and on the streets. 

SecTION VIII.—The Boarding House Committee shall keep a register of re- 
spectable and well kept boarding houses. They shall visit as far as possible these 
boarding houses, and invite the young men to attend the Association. This list shall 
be revised once every six months. 

SecTIon IX.—The Literary and Social Work Committee shall provide the 
programme for the regular monthly meetings of the Association, and arrange for such 
other Social Receptions as may be ordered by the Association. They will make 
provision for a course of Literary meetings or Reading Circle for the mutual improve- 
ment of the members of the Association, 

Secrion X.—The Strangers Tea Committee will provide for a Social Tea to be 
served on Sunday evenings, to which stranger young men in the city will be invited, 
and afterwards introduced to the City Churches of their choice. 

SECTION XI.—The Committee on Visiting Sick Young Men shall attend promptly 
to all calls upon them, and seek to cheer and aid them during sickness. When 
necessary they shall also provide ‘‘ watchers” to sit up during the night. 

SECTION XII.—All the Committees of the Association are appointed for the pur- 
pose of aiding inthe work of more effectively reaching and saving young men. If any 
Committee stands in the way of accomplishing these objects, the Board shall disband 
such Committee. If any member or members of a Committee are hindering its useful- 
ness the President shall have power to remove him or them from such Committee. 

SECTION XIIJ.—AIl Committees shall notify the General Secretary of their 
meetings. 

SECTION XIV.—It shall be the imperative duty of all the Committees of the 
Association to organize immediately after their appointment, elect a Secretary, and 
keep correct minutes of all their proceedings, to decide what stated meetings they will 
hold during the year. 

SECTION XV.—It shall also be the duty of all Committees of the Association to 
report in writing to the Association once a month. The Board shall have the right to 
call for a report from any of the Committees at any time. 


ARTICLE XII.—DISCIPLINE. 

No person shall hold any office or position of trust in this Association who shall 
cease to profess and practice the fundamental doctrines of Evangelical Christianity, 
and the Board of Directors shall have full power to investigate any questions of the 
doctrines or conduct of any officer or member of the Association, and upon a two-third 
(24) vote of the Board such officer or member may be removed from office or 
membership. 

ARTICLE XIIJ.—AMENDMENTS. 

SEcTION I.—These By-Laws may be amended by a two-third (24) vote of the 
members present at any regular meeting of the Association, notice having been given 
at a previous regular meeting of the proposed amendment. 

SecTion II.—Any By-Law may be suspended bya two-third (24) vote of the 
members present at any regular business meeting.
